name: Actor Model Concurrency
tagline: Share-nothing concurrent entities communicating exclusively via asynchronous immutable messages and per-actor mailboxes.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of the Actor Model—from share-nothing mailboxes to supervision trees, backpressure, and cluster sharding.

spark.summary: The Actor Model structures concurrent systems as isolated, share-nothing entities (actors) that encapsulate private state and communicate exclusively via asynchronous message passing into per-actor mailboxes (e.g., Erlang/OTP GenServer, Akka/Pekko, Microsoft Orleans).
spark.keyTakeaway: To guarantee worst-case bounds under adversarial inputs, by processing one message at a time per actor and forbidding shared mutable memory, you eliminate mutexes and deadlocks—trading synchronous call convenience for mailbox backpressure and supervision trees.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Proposed by Carl Hewitt in 1973 and battle-tested in Ericsson's AXD301 ATM switches (99.9999999% uptime), the **Actor Model** treats the *actor*—not the thread or lock—as the fundamental unit of computation.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Single-Threaded Mailbox Turn & Supervision State Machine (IDLE -> ACTIVE TURN -> SUPERVISED); Asynchronous Tell Flow vs. Synchronous Ask Deadlock (WS Gateway -> Shard Coord -> OrderBook(BTC)); 3-Node Actor Cluster with Quorum Split-Brain Resolver (Shard Coordinator -> Worker Node 1 -> Worker Node 2).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Actor runtimes differ in scheduling, state lifecycle, and typing. In a distributed digital-twin or exchange cluster, **Cluster Sharding** hashes `entity_id` across worker nodes so each active entity runs on exactly one node, while a **quorum Split-Brain Resolver** downs minority partitions cleanly.

**Failure Modes & Application:** By processing one message at a time per actor and forbidding shared mutable memory, you eliminate mutexes and deadlocks—trading synchronous call convenience for mailbox backpressure and supervision trees.

learningJourney.title: What is Actor Model Concurrency

explanation.foundation: Proposed by Carl Hewitt in 1973 and battle-tested in Ericsson's AXD301 ATM switches (99.9999999% uptime), the **Actor Model** treats the *actor*—not the thread or lock—as the fundamental unit of computation. An actor combines **private state**, a **behavior** (message handler), and a **mailbox** (FIFO queue).
explanation.core: On receiving a message, an actor can do three primitives: **send** finite messages to known actors, **spawn** new actors, or **designate** the behavior for the next message. Because no actor can inspect another actor's memory and each processes one message at a time, torn reads and lock-order deadlocks disappear by construction.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Actors (and why shared-memory locks fail at scale)

explanation.foundation: Shared-memory multithreading forces developers to reason about lock ordering, memory barriers, and cache-line false sharing across every call site.
explanation.core: Actors invert this: **state is partitioned by entity**, and **location transparency** (`pid ! msg` or `actorRef.tell(msg)`) uses the exact same syntax whether the target actor lives in the same OS process or on another cluster node.
explanation.deepDive: However, synchronous `ask` chains (`A asks B`, `B asks A`) reintroduce deadlocks—so production actor systems default to asynchronous `tell`.

sectionDiagram.summary: Asynchronous tell with correlation IDs keeps mailboxes non-blocking; synchronous mutual ask deadlocks both actors.

ideas.title: Preemptive vs. Cooperative Scheduling
ideas.description: Erlang BEAM uses reduction-based preemptive scheduling (~4,000 reductions/slice), preventing starvation; JVM/CLR frameworks (Pekko, Orleans) are cooperative, so blocking I/O inside onReceive starves sibling actors.

ideas.title: Supervision Trees
ideas.description: Parents never share memory with children; they observe exit signals and apply One-For-One, All-For-One, or Escalate policies within max_restarts budgets.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Actor Model Concurrency without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: To guarantee worst-case bounds under adversarial inputs, by processing one message at a time per actor and forbidding shared mutable memory, you eliminate mutexes and deadlocks—trading synchronous call convenience for mailbox backpressure and supervision trees.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Where the Actor Model shines (and where to avoid it)** as the intuition layer for Actor Model Concurrency: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.
explanation.core: Actors excel when millions of **stateful, independent entities** (chat rooms, IoT digital twins, game sessions, order books) receive concurrent events and must maintain strict per-entity ordering without external lock contention.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, where the actor model shines (and where to avoid it) becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. The Actor Model structures concurrent systems as isolated, share-nothing entities (actors) that encapsulate private state and communicate exclusively via asynchronous message passing into per-actor mailboxes (e.g., Erlang/OTP GenServer, Akka/Pekko, Microsoft Orleans).

comparison.choice: Stateful Digital Twins & IoT / Gaming Sessions
benefits: One actor per device/session holds hot state in RAM with zero mutexes and automatic cluster sharding.
costs: Requires event sourcing or periodic snapshots to reconstruct RAM state after node restarts.

benefits: Preemptive scheduling and per-process GC isolate latency spikes across millions of connections.
costs: CPU-heavy numerical/SIMD math is slower on BEAM unless offloaded to Rustler NIFs.

comparison.choice: Avoid: Stateless CRUD & Bulk Analytical Joins
benefits: Use stateless HTTP services + SQL/columnar engines instead of wrapping simple DB rows in actors.
costs: Actor indirection adds serialization and mailbox latency without solving a concurrency problem.

learningJourney.title: How Actor Mailboxes, Persistence, and Backpressure are managed

explanation.foundation: Operating actors in production requires guarding against **unbounded mailboxes**, **blocking I/O**, and **split-brain clusters**:
explanation.core:
1. **Bounded Mailboxes & Backpressure**: Configure bounded mailboxes and bridge Kafka/TCP ingress with demand-driven streams (`GenStage`, `Pekko Streams`).
2. **Isolated Blocking Dispatchers**: Offload synchronous JDBC/HTTP calls onto dedicated I/O thread pools.
3. **Event Sourcing + Snapshots**: Persist state transitions to an append-only journal.
4. **Split-Brain Resolver (SBR)**: Enable a quorum-based SBR before deploying Cluster Sharding.

knowledgeCheck.question: In an Akka/Pekko actor system, Actor A handles a message by calling `ask(Actor B)` synchronously while Actor B is simultaneously calling `ask(Actor A)`. What happens?

options.text: Both actors deadlock until their ask timeouts expire
options.feedback: Correct: because each actor processes one message at a time, neither can pop the incoming ask from its mailbox while blocked waiting for the reply.

options.text: The mailbox automatically prioritizes reply messages ahead of requests
options.feedback: Standard FIFO mailboxes do not preempt an active synchronous block; you must use asynchronous tell with correlation IDs.

options.text: The supervisor immediately restarts both actors
options.feedback: Supervisors only act on exceptions/crashes, not blocked futures waiting on a timeout.
